title: Dead Men Vote Tuesday
subtitle: Kansas City, Election Week, October and November 1936

listing.title: Dead Men Vote Tuesday 🎷
listing.blurb: Kansas City, election week, 1936. The town is wide open, the machine counts the votes, and on 18th Street the best piano player in the Gold Leaf Club walked out after the last set and never got home. His band has forty dollars and no one else to ask. His dead mother is registered to vote at an empty lot, the rolls are full of ghosts, and a nervous man from the Election Board wants his little black book back before Tuesday. Levels 3–6.

synopsis: Kansas City, Missouri, in the autumn of 1936 is the most wide-open town between Chicago and the coast. Repeal is three years old and nobody ever really obeyed Prohibition here anyway; the clubs on Twelfth Street never close, the dice tables are in the front windows, and the city, the county and the police department all answer to one political machine, run from a plain two-storey office on Main Street by a bonding-company man named Sidney 'Big Sid' Varnum. Every city contractor needs a Varnum bond, every saloon needs a Varnum licence, and every election the machine wins by more than the year before. Two miles east, at Eighteenth and Vine, is the other Kansas City: the heart of Black Kansas City, a few blocks of clubs, churches, barbershops, a hotel, a ballroom and a musicians' union hall, where the bands play until breakfast and the best music in America is being invented by people who cannot buy a sandwich at a downtown lunch counter. On Tuesday 3 November the nation votes, Roosevelt or Landon on the radio, and the machine has promised Jefferson City and Washington the biggest majority in the city's history. In the early hours of Sunday 25 October, Julius 'Jules' Ransom, pianist and leader of the ten-piece house band at the Gold Leaf Club on Eighteenth Street, played the last set, walked out to his car at ten past four, and vanished. The police say a colored musician who stays out late is not a missing person. On Monday morning his singer, Geneva Hollins, brings the band's kitty, forty dollars in small bills, to a private detective's office over a barbershop on Eighteenth Street. The truth is that Jules is in police custody under a false name, moved from station to station so that no lawyer can find him, because on Saturday night he lifted a black clothbound book from the overcoat of Virgil Strode, the machine's registration man at the Board of Election Commissioners. The book is the working plan of the ghost vote in the Second and Fourth Wards: 1,108 dead people, nearly all of them Black, taken from the city's own death certificates and registered at vacant lots and burned-out houses, each with the name of the white flophouse repeater from the river wards who will vote them on Tuesday, and at the back, the cash. Jules's mother, dead since February 1935, is on page eleven. Without the book, Strode's repeaters do not know which names to vote, and Strode cannot rebuild it by Tuesday. Over two weeks the party must find the missing man before he is taken for a ride; walk a precinct where the dead outnumber the living; find the book before the machine does; stand in a barbershop polling place on election day while the ghosts vote and the living are turned away; and then, with the machine victorious and the federal government suddenly interested, decide what to do with a book that could put a few rich men in prison, or a few hundred poor ones, or no one at all, and that has the names of the dead of Eighteenth Street written in it in a stranger's hand.
hook: Monday 26 October 1936, eleven in the morning, Eighteenth Street. The office of Matthias Hartsell, Confidential Investigations, is one room over Dandridge's Barber Shop, and the radio downstairs is playing the President's speech from Saturday for the third time. In the barbershop window, under the striped pole, a sheet of paper has been pasted to the glass: OFFICIAL REGISTER OF QUALIFIED VOTERS, PRECINCT 14, SECOND WARD, every name in this part of the city in small type. The stairs creak. The woman who comes in is the singer from the Gold Leaf Club, Geneva Hollins, in a church hat and a coat too thin for the weather, and she puts a cigar box on the desk and opens it: forty dollars in ones and fives and a few silver dollars, the band's kitty. Jules Ransom went out of the Gold Leaf at ten past four on Sunday morning with his hat on and his music under his arm, and nobody has seen him since. His car is gone. His rooms have been torn apart. The police at Number Four District told her to go home. 'He doesn't drink, he doesn't owe, and he doesn't miss a downbeat,' she says. 'We play again Thursday. If he's not on that piano bench on Thursday, there's no band, and there's ten men and their families with no work in the winter. And if he's dead, I want to know who.' Across the street, a green Ford with two white men in it has been parked outside the Gold Leaf since nine o'clock, which on Eighteenth Street is the same as hanging out a sign.

setting.name: Kansas City, Missouri, Monday 26 October to Saturday 7 November 1936
setting.description: The city is real, and so are its places and its year; the machine, its boss, its men and every person in this campaign are fictional. Kansas City sits on the bluffs where the Kansas River runs into the Missouri, a city of stockyards, railroads, grain elevators and boulevards, half Southern and half Western, with a population of four hundred thousand and the appetite of a town twice the size. Union Station, the second-biggest railway station in the country, faces the Liberty Memorial across a lawn. Downtown is rising out of the Depression on public money: the new Jackson County Courthouse is two years old, the new City Hall tower is going up on Twelfth Street, and the Municipal Auditorium is being finished, every one of them built by contractors bonded by Varnum. Twelfth Street is the white entertainment district, a mile of nightclubs, taxi-dance halls, dice rooms and burlesque that never close. North, along the river, are the river wards: rail yards, produce markets, flophouses that rent a cot for fifteen cents a night, and the men who live in them, who vote wherever they are told for two dollars a time. South are the Country Club District and Ward Parkway: fountains, stone houses, deed restrictions that say who may never live there. East, past the Paseo, is Eighteenth and Vine. Kansas City is a segregated city by law and by custom. Black children go to separate schools; Black patients go to General Hospital Number Two or to Wheatley-Provident, the private hospital Black doctors built because the city would not; Black customers may spend money at downtown stores and may not try on a hat or sit at the counter; Black musicians belong to their own union, Local 627, because the white local will not have them; a handful of Black patrolmen walk the Eighteenth Street beats and are not, by the department's unwritten rule, to lay hands on a white man. None of this is scenery. It is a set of locked doors, a daily insult and a source of fury, and the people who live behind it run churches, newspapers, businesses, ward clubs, numbers banks and the best bands in America, and have their own interests, quarrels and plans.
setting.atmosphere: Wind. Kansas City in late autumn is cold dry wind off the plains, leaves in the gutters, the smell of the stockyards when it blows from the west and of barbecue smoke when it does not. Brick and limestone, streetcars sparking, election posters on every pole, sound trucks playing 'Happy Days Are Here Again' and 'Oh! Susanna' for Landon. Radios in every window, and on Eighteenth Street, music out of every door: a piano at a rent party, a trumpet practising scales over a shoeshine stand, a twelve-piece band rehearsing in a ballroom at noon, and at four in the morning the jam session at the union hall where the musicians play for each other and nobody is paid. The tone is hard-boiled paperback: cigarette smoke, rye, rain on a car roof, a split lip, blood on a cell floor, a ward heeler's handshake with a two-dollar bill in it. Everyone is compromised and almost nobody is a monster. The music matters. Describe it. Let it comment on the scenes: a ballad in a near-empty club at dawn, a cutting contest that goes on for an hour, a band playing for its life on Thursday night with someone else at the piano.

regions.name: Eighteenth and Vine
regions.description: The heart of Black Kansas City and of the music. The Gold Leaf Club on Eighteenth Street just west of Vine, owned by Mrs. Willa Templeton: a long room with a pressed-tin ceiling, a bandstand, a bar, a coat check, a back room with a card table and a door to the alley. Dandridge's Barber Shop, which is also the polling place of Precinct 14 of the Second Ward, with Matthias Hartsell's office upstairs. The Lincoln Arms Hotel, where Jules Ransom keeps two rooms on the third floor. The Musicians' union hall on Highland, Local 627, where the jam sessions start at four in the morning. Paseo Hall, the big ballroom. Churches: Mount Gilead Baptist, whose pastor buries half the neighbourhood. Wheatley-Provident Hospital, a few blocks away. The Vine Street Democratic Club, Horace Quarterman's ward club, over a furniture store, where the coal tickets, city jobs and Christmas baskets come from.

regions.name: Downtown and the Machine
regions.description: The Board of Election Commissioners in the old City Hall, where Virgil Strode keeps the registration books and the Health Department keeps the death certificates two floors down. Police Headquarters and the district stations: Number Four (Eighteenth Street's station), Number Six in Westport, Number Two by the river. The Jackson County Courthouse, where Judge Orville Stanfield's courtroom handles writs of habeas corpus. Varnum Bonding and Surety on Main Street, two storeys, plain brick, a line of men in hats outside it every morning waiting to ask for something. The Muehlebach Hotel, where the machine's guests stay and where a Black man can enter by the service door only. The Kansas City Monitor, the reform evening paper, on Grand Avenue.

regions.name: Twelfth Street and the River Wards
regions.description: Twelfth Street at night is neon, dice, taxi-dancers at ten cents a dance and Black bands playing for white crowds who would not let them through the front door anywhere else. North of downtown, down the bluff toward the Missouri, are the river wards: the City Market, the rail yards, and the flophouses of Fifth Street, chief among them the Burnham Hotel, four floors of cots run by Harvey Gleason, the machine's First Ward precinct captain, whose residents are the repeaters. On election day the floater cars leave from the Burnham's back lot before dawn.

regions.name: Union Station, the Liberty Memorial and the Country Club District
regions.description: Union Station, vast and marble, where the trains go to Chicago, St. Louis and the coast and where, three years ago, men were shot dead on the plaza in a gangland massacre the city still talks about. Across the lawn on its hill, the Liberty Memorial's tower and its flame. South along Ward Parkway, the Country Club District: Beatrice Albright's family house, the country club, and the deed restrictions in every title, written by the men who built it, saying who may never own a house there.

campaignRules.name: The Calendar
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a fixed calendar and the opposition acts on it whether or not the players are watching. bn-scenario-001 is Monday 26 and Tuesday 27 October; bn-scenario-002 is Wednesday 28 October to Saturday 31 October (Halloween); bn-scenario-003 is Monday 2 November and election day, Tuesday 3 November, to the end of the count at about 2 a.m.; bn-scenario-004 is Wednesday 4 to Saturday 7 November. The unit of time is the scene, about two hours; a day has six to eight scenes from breakfast to the last set, and a trip across town, a stakeout or an hour in a records room costs one. Say the time when the party arrives anywhere. If nobody interferes, this happens. MONDAY: Jules Ransom is moved from Number Four District to Number Six in Westport, booked as 'J. Rand'. TUESDAY: Ogden Fry, the Health Department clerk who sold Strode the death certificates, telephones the federal man Thomas Merriwether from a drugstore and asks to meet on Thursday; at 11 p.m. Lt. Conrad Voyles throws him from the fire escape of the old City Hall. WEDNESDAY: Fry is found at 7 a.m.; Jules is moved to Number Two District by the river as 'Julian Rance'. THURSDAY: Strode's men search Geneva Hollins's room; the band plays the Gold Leaf without Jules. FRIDAY: Lucky Bowden's drum trunk sits in the union hall basement with the book inside it. SATURDAY 31 OCTOBER, 3 a.m.: Voyles releases Jules out of the back of Number Two District to Harvey Gleason's men; on the river bluff they beat the location of the book out of him and shoot him 'escaping'; at 5 a.m. they take the trunk from the union hall. MONDAY: Strode hands out the assignments. TUESDAY: the ghosts vote. WEDNESDAY: Varnum decides Strode is a federal witness waiting to happen. THURSDAY: a professional checks into the Muehlebach. FRIDAY night: Strode is found dead in his hotel room, a 'suicide', and the book is ash. Whatever the players change, the people they have not touched carry on, adapting only to what they could plausibly know.

campaignRules.name: Heat
campaignRules.description: The party has a single Heat score for Kansas City, 0 to 10, tracked openly by the GM and announced whenever it changes. It starts at 1, because a green Ford has been watching the Gold Leaf since Sunday. It rises by 1 for being seen somewhere you should not be, leaning on the wrong man (a cop, a ward captain, an Election Board clerk, anyone at Varnum Bonding), a fistfight in public, or a story with the party's names in it; by 2 for gunfire, a car chase the police see, breaking into a building or a station house; by 3 for a body. It falls by 1 for each half-day spent quietly and by 1 when the party does someone powerful a favour. At Heat 3 the cops start asking: plainclothesmen tail the party, the desk sergeants stop taking money, and any Black member of the party is stopped and searched on sight downtown. At Heat 6 someone is told to take care of you: Harvey Gleason sends three men with bats, and Lem Castle (if played) is suspended or transferred to the stockyards beat. At Heat 9 the city is closed to you: licences pulled, a warrant on a pretext, and no cabbie, clerk or doorman on either side of the color line will help. Heat is the machine's attention, not the neighbourhood's. Doing right by Eighteenth Street never raises it.

campaignRules.name: The Three-Clue Rule
campaignRules.description: Every conclusion the players need to reach has at least three clues pointing to it, in different places, and every scenario names them. The campaign's conclusions are lettered A to H in the control file. Core clues are found automatically by anyone who looks in the right place with the right skill: no roll. Rolls add detail, save a scene or avoid Heat; a failed roll never dead-ends the case, it costs time, a favour or a point of Heat. When the players are stuck, use the case board: Matthias Hartsell's office has a corkboard, and Geneva Hollins has a way of asking 'So what do we actually know?' Summarize out loud the suspects, what each is known to want, the open questions and the leads not yet followed.

campaignRules.name: The Color Line
campaignRules.description: Kansas City in 1936 is segregated, and the campaign treats segregation as the injustice it was, never as decoration or as a penalty to make a character weaker. In play it works like this. Doors: downtown hotels, restaurants, white clubs and the front rows of theatres are closed to Black characters (service entrances and balconies only), and the GM says so plainly when it happens, through a specific person, not as an abstraction. The reverse is also real: a white character on Eighteenth Street is conspicuous, gets polite answers and no information until someone vouches for them, and is assumed to be a cop, a slummer or a machine man. Authority: Lem Castle's badge works on Eighteenth Street and stops at the color line by the department's unwritten rule, and he knows the cost of crossing it. Danger: a Black man alone downtown after dark, or in a police station, is in more danger than a white man in the same place, and the GM plays that honestly. Never: no slurs from anyone, ever; period terms of the polite kind ('colored', 'Negro') appear only on signs, forms and newspaper pages and in the speech of people of the time, and the GM's own narration says Black. Black characters are never comic relief, never menace, never helpless and never a lesson for a white character. Each has their own interests, and some of them are at odds with the party's.

campaignRules.name: The Merry-Go-Round
campaignRules.description: Jules Ransom is not in any jail under his own name. Lt. Conrad Voyles of Homicide is holding him 'for investigation', which in this city means no charge, no lawyer and no telephone call, and moving him every day or two from one district station to another under a different misspelled name, so that a writ of habeas corpus naming Julius Ransom finds nobody. Sunday and Monday: Number Four District, as 'John Ransome'; Monday night to Wednesday: Number Six in Westport, as 'J. Rand'; Wednesday to Saturday: Number Two by the river, as 'Julian Rance'. To find him the party needs the current station and the current name; to get him out, a lawyer, a writ and a judge who will sign it (Hezekiah Wilburn, Esq., and Judge Orville Stanfield), or a bribe in the hundreds, or a favour from a man who outranks Voyles, or nerve. Each move is a chance: the prisoner van, the booking desk, the trusties who carry the meals and count the plates. Jules is being questioned hard. Each day he is held, he begins scenes with 2 fewer hit points (to a minimum of half), and he will not tell anyone in a uniform where the book is, because he knows that the moment he does, he is no longer worth keeping alive.

campaignRules.name: Election Day
campaignRules.description: The polls are open from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Tuesday 3 November. At each precinct there are four judges and two clerks, two of each from each party, and in the machine's precincts the 'Republican' judges are usually machine men too; at Precinct 14 one of them is not. Before dawn the floater cars leave the Burnham Hotel lot with five repeaters each. Each repeater carries a slip with a ghost's name and address from the book, votes, is paid two dollars at the car, and goes to the next precinct; a good crew votes eight or ten times a day. Repeaters also vote the names of living people who have not come in yet, so that when a living voter arrives at four in the afternoon, the clerk says 'You've already voted', and the challenge goes nowhere. Catching it: a living witness turned away, a repeater with a slip in his pocket, the poll book signature of a dead woman, a floater car's route. Each of these is evidence; with the book it is proof. After 7 p.m. the count: ballots are tallied at the precinct and the tally sheets signed by the judges and carried downtown, and in the machine's precincts the count is a performance. Heat on election day rises double for anything seen by a cop. The machine wins regardless. What the players decide is what can be proved, and against whom.

campaignRules.name: Prices
campaignRules.description: These are Depression prices and people are hungry: the bribe table in investigation.json applies at the same prices, and anyone poor enough to take a bribe takes the going rate with advantage on any check. A cup of coffee and a doughnut is ten cents, a cab across town forty cents, a streetcar seven, a payphone a nickel, a room at the Lincoln Arms a dollar a night, a cot at the Burnham fifteen cents, a repeater's vote two dollars, a floater driver's day five, a precinct captain's election-day envelope fifty, a desk sergeant ten, a lost booking card twenty-five. Matthias Hartsell's fee is ten dollars a day and expenses; the band's forty dollars buys four days. Favours run on two systems that do not trust each other: the machine's (a job, a coal ticket, a licence, a dropped charge, a writ ignored) and Eighteenth Street's own (a church, a lodge, a numbers banker, a doctor, a union hall, a newspaper that never names a source). A Fixer's favours may be drawn from either, and the GM notes which; spending a machine favour on Eighteenth Street is remembered there.

explorationRules: This is a city campaign and the map is a schematic of Kansas City: Eighteenth and Vine to the east, downtown and the old City Hall in the middle, the river wards and the Burnham Hotel to the north, Union Station and the Liberty Memorial to the south of downtown, Ward Parkway far to the south. The party moves by Cleve Marchbanks's cab if he is played, by streetcar, on foot or by borrowed car, and the unit of time is the scene, roughly two hours. The calendar (see campaignRules) is the engine: every scene spent somewhere is a scene not spent somewhere else, and the people the party has not touched keep moving. Run each day as a small sandbox of named places listed in that day's scenario, with each person acting on their own schedule and on what they could know. Nobody is omniscient: Varnum knows what Strode and Voyles tell him, Voyles knows what his station houses and his informants see, Quarterman knows everything on Eighteenth Street and nothing downtown, and Strode knows only that he is in trouble. Investigation follows the three-clue rule: core clues are automatic; rolls add detail or speed; failure costs time, Heat or a favour, never the case. The color line (see campaignRules) shapes which party members can go where and who will talk to them, and splitting the party along it is often the fastest way to work and the most dangerous. Fights are short, ugly and rare; most scenes are conversations in bad light with someone who wants something. Between scenes let the city breathe: a sound truck playing Roosevelt's song, the smell of hickory smoke from a barbecue stand on Eighteenth, the stockyards on the west wind, a streetcar bell, the rehearsal through the wall at Paseo Hall, the four a.m. jam session, a radio in a cell block playing the election returns.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, it does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. Kansas City, its streets and landmarks (Eighteenth and Vine, the Paseo, the Musicians' union hall of Local 627 on Highland, Wheatley-Provident Hospital, General Hospital Number Two, Union Station, the Liberty Memorial, the Muehlebach Hotel, Twelfth Street, the City Market, Ward Parkway) are real, and so are the year, the 3 November 1936 election, the city's machine politics in general, its segregation, the 1933 Union Station shootings and the violent spring election of 1934. The machine, Varnum Bonding and Surety, the Gold Leaf Club, the Lincoln Arms Hotel, the Burnham Hotel, the Vine Street Democratic Club, the Kansas City Monitor and every person in this campaign are fictional. No real politician, gangster, musician or private individual appears; Roosevelt and Landon are on the radio and nowhere else. The ledger, its numbers and the deaths in this story are invented.
controlFile.theTruth: Kansas City's machine has padded the registration rolls for years; for 1936 Big Sid Varnum has promised his friends in Jefferson City and Washington the biggest majority in the city's history, and the man who builds the padding is Virgil Strode, 47, deputy chief clerk of the Board of Election Commissioners. In the Second and Fourth Wards, the Black wards east of the Paseo, Strode's ghosts are the dead. Since the spring he has bought copies of the Health Department's death certificates for 1928 to 1936 from a records clerk, Ogden Fry, at ten dollars a hundred, picking from the column the certificates mark 'colored', because, as he told Fry, 'nobody downtown ever checks a colored death', and registered 1,108 of the dead at addresses that are vacant lots, burned houses, a coal yard and a church, each name in a precinct where a machine captain will see it voted. The hands that vote them are not Black. They are 212 white men from the flophouses of the river wards, chiefly the Burnham Hotel on Fifth Street, run by the First Ward captain Harvey Gleason, who will be driven east in floater cars on election day and paid two dollars a vote. Strode keeps the whole operation in one black clothbound book: page by page, ghost name, false address, precinct, the repeater crew assigned, and at the back the cash, $11,400 in seven payments since June, each signed for with the initials of Norbert Varnum, Big Sid's nephew and the treasurer of Varnum Bonding and Surety. Without the book Strode cannot run Tuesday; he never made a copy, because a copy is evidence. On Saturday night 24 October Strode took the book to the Gold Leaf Club, where he is a Saturday regular at the white tables near the bandstand (he loves the music, which is the only uncomplicated thing about him), to meet two Second Ward precinct captains in the back room after hours and give them their lists. He checked his overcoat with the book in it. Julius 'Jules' Ransom, the bandleader, had already seen Lavinia Ransom, his mother, who died of pneumonia at Wheatley-Provident in February 1935, listed on the Precinct 14 register in Dandridge's window at 1712 Woodland, a lot that has been empty since a fire in 1931. He had asked Horace Quarterman, the Second Ward leader, about it in September, and Quarterman told him to leave it alone and mentioned, too casually, the clerk's name and the book. At 2:40 on Sunday morning, in the set break, Jules saw the clothbound book in the pocket of the camel overcoat on the coat-check rail while the coat-check girl, Zora Lattimore, was in the kitchen; he took it, read it in the band room, found his mother on page eleven, and understood what it was. He wrapped it in his band shirt and handed it to his drummer, Leander 'Lucky' Bowden, at 4:05 with the words 'Hold my laundry, Lucky, I'll get it Thursday'; Lucky stuffed it into the bass-drum trunk without looking and took the trunk to the union hall basement on Highland, where the band's instruments are stored. Strode found the book gone at 3:50 and asked Zora who had been near the rail; she said only the band. Strode telephoned Lt. Conrad Voyles of Homicide, the machine's man in the police. Voyles leaned on Zora, who is Horace Quarterman's niece; Quarterman, called out of bed at 4 a.m., told Voyles it must have been Jules, because Jules had been asking about the rolls, and gave him up to save Zora, on Voyles's promise that Jules would only be held until after the election. Voyles's men took Jules at 4:10 at his car outside the club. He has been held since on the merry-go-round (see campaignRules), questioned with fists and a rubber hose, and has said nothing, because he understands that the book is the only reason he is alive. Voyles has no intention of keeping Quarterman's promise. On Tuesday night, 27 October, Ogden Fry, frightened by Jules's disappearance and by a federal agent asking about death certificates, telephoned Special Agent Thomas Merriwether of the FBI to arrange a meeting; Voyles, whose man on the City Hall switchboard listens to the drugstore line, met Fry on the old City Hall fire escape at 11 p.m. and threw him off it. If nobody interferes, on the early morning of Saturday 31 October Voyles hands Jules out of the back of Number Two District to Gleason's men, who beat the location of the book out of him on the river bluff and shoot him; the book is recovered from the union hall at 5 a.m.; the ghosts vote on Tuesday; and the machine wins by its biggest margin ever. Then the machine turns on itself. With federal agents in town and an election to account for, Varnum decides on Wednesday 4 November that Strode, who knows everything and is visibly coming apart, is a liability, and that the book, which carries his nephew's initials, must cease to exist. He sends to St. Louis for a professional, who registers at the Muehlebach on Thursday as Mr. Everett Brumley, a seed salesman. Strode, who has worked out what he is worth to the government, is trying at the same time to sell himself and the book to Agent Merriwether for immunity. On Friday night, if nobody interferes, Brumley kills Strode in his room at the Hotel Savoy and burns the book in the bathroom basin; the federal case that follows is built on what Merriwether can see, which is ghost votes in the Black wards, and is brought against the small men closest to hand: two Black precinct captains, the floater drivers, a few repeaters, and the dead.
suspects: Lt. Conrad Voyles, 51, Homicide: the machine's man in the police department. Holds Jules on the merry-go-round, killed Ogden Fry, and intends Jules to die. Use Bent Detective. Patient, polite, soft-handed, a deacon at a white church in the Northeast, and as close to a monster as this campaign has.

Virgil Strode, 47, deputy chief clerk of the Board of Election Commissioners: built the ghost vote and lost the book. Nervous, fussy, a widower who loves the music on Eighteenth Street and sees no contradiction. Not a killer; becomes, in bn-scenario-004, the most important witness in the city and a dead man walking.

Sidney 'Big Sid' Varnum, 63, the boss: owns Varnum Bonding and Surety and, through it, the city. Never touches anything. Fights through other people; use Mob Boss. Wants the margin on Tuesday and the book gone on Wednesday.

Horace Quarterman, 58, leader of the Second Ward and the Vine Street Democratic Club: gave Jules up to save his niece Zora, believed Voyles's promise, and has not slept since. Delivers coal, jobs, bail and Christmas baskets, and the vote. Believes the machine is the only power in the city that has ever given Eighteenth Street anything, and that it can be managed. He wants the book found and burned, because his own precinct captains are in it.
Harvey Gleason, 44, First Ward precinct captain and manager of the Burnham Hotel: supplies the repeaters and the muscle, and sends men after the book. Use Mob Lieutenant.
Mr. Everett Brumley, the professional from St. Louis, arrives on Thursday 5 November: use The Professional. Courteous, colourless, wears a grey suit and reads seed catalogues in the Muehlebach lobby.
redHerrings: Willa Templeton, the Gold Leaf's owner, pays the machine for her liquor licence every Monday, had a loud argument with Jules on Saturday about playing a machine rally, and has been seen at Varnum Bonding. She looks like the woman who sold him out. She is paying, like every club owner on Eighteenth Street, and she is frightened for her licence and her staff, and she is on Jules's side.

Casey Dudek (if not a player character, any Gleason man) has been asking around Eighteenth Street for 'a book a colored piano player took'. He looks like the man who took Jules. He was hired on Sunday, after it happened.

The federal man, Thomas Merriwether, is asking questions about death certificates and was seen with Ogden Fry; some on Eighteenth Street think he is the machine's spy. He is what he says he is, and his interest is real, and so is the danger that his case will land on the wrong people.

Rumour on Eighteenth Street says Jules owed money to a numbers banker and ran. He owes nobody. The rumour was started at the Vine Street Democratic Club, by Quarterman, to explain an absence he knows the reason for.
clues: A. JULES WAS TAKEN BY THE POLICE AND IS HELD OFF THE BOOKS ON THE MERRY-GO-ROUND. A1: Cleve Marchbanks (or the shoeshine boy Tadpole, who sleeps in the club's doorway) saw two white men in a green Ford show a badge and put Jules in the back seat at 4:10 on Sunday (bn-scenario-001). A2: Jules's 1934 Terraplane is in the police impound lot, towed Sunday at 6 a.m. on a Number Four District slip with no case number (bn-scenario-001). A3: the jail trusties carry the meals and count the plates: one extra plate in the Number Four cells Sunday and Monday for a prisoner listed as 'John Ransome, hold for Lt. V.' (bn-scenario-001). A4: Dr. Mayhew is called to Number Four on Monday night to treat a 'colored prisoner who fell', and it is Jules (bn-scenario-001). A5: the booking cards at Number Six and Number Two, 'J. Rand' and 'Julian Rance', in the same desk sergeant's hand (bn-scenario-002).

B. JULES TOOK SOMETHING FROM VIRGIL STRODE: THE BOOK. B1: Jules's rooms at the Lincoln Arms were searched professionally on Sunday afternoon: mattress cut, piano roll cabinet emptied, every book shaken; the desk clerk was paid $5 to forget two white men (bn-scenario-001). B2: Zora Lattimore, the coat-check girl, says a white man in a camel coat lost 'a book' from his pocket and that the police leaned on her (bn-scenario-001). B3: Beatrice Albright saw the man in the camel coat on Saturday night and knows his face: Virgil Strode of the Election Board (bn-scenario-001). B4: Casey Dudek's errand, or any Gleason man's, is to find 'a black book a colored piano player took' (bn-scenario-001 or 002).

C. THE GHOST VOTERS ARE THE DEAD OF BLACK KANSAS CITY, REGISTERED AT FALSE ADDRESSES. C1: the Precinct 14 register in Dandridge's window lists Lavinia Ransom at 1712 Woodland, an empty lot (bn-scenario-001). C2: Dr. Mayhew signed Lavinia Ransom's death certificate in February 1935; the hospital copy is in Wheatley-Provident's records (bn-scenario-001). C3: Jules's own list, hidden in his music, of thirty-one names from the register with their dates of death from Mount Gilead's burial book (bn-scenario-001). C4: walking Precinct 14: forty-four voters registered at a coal yard, nineteen at a church, eleven at a burned house; every name is someone Reverend Zebulon Pettus buried (bn-scenario-002). C5: the Health Department's death-certificate drawers: the 'colored' files for 1928 to 1936 have been taken out and copied, and the copying-room log shows Fry working nights (bn-scenario-002).

D. THE BOOK IS IN LUCKY BOWDEN'S BASS-DRUM TRUNK AT THE UNION HALL. D1: Geneva Hollins saw Jules give Lucky a bundled shirt at 4:05 (bn-scenario-001, if she is asked about the last minutes). D2: a note smuggled out of Number Six by a trusty, in Jules's hand: 'Tell Lucky to wash my shirt before Thursday' (bn-scenario-002). D3: the band boy, Pete Greenlee, says Lucky's trunk was 'heavy as a Bible' going down the union hall stairs (bn-scenario-002). D4: Jules himself, once free and among people he trusts (bn-scenario-002).

E. OGDEN FRY WAS MURDERED BY LT. VOYLES. E1: Fry's body is on the areaway below the fire escape, but his hat and his reading glasses are on the fourth-floor landing, folded, and the window was latched from inside (bn-scenario-002). E2: the night janitor, Mr. Odell Swann, was sent home at 10:30 by 'a detective in a grey hat with a gold tooth' (bn-scenario-002). E3: the telephone-exchange operator connected Fry to the federal building at 6:15 on Tuesday, and the City Hall switchboard man who listens to that line reports to Voyles (bn-scenario-002). E4: Voyles's knuckles, Wednesday: skinned on the right hand, and fire-escape rust on his coat cuff (Forensics, bn-scenario-002).

F. THE GHOSTS ARE VOTED BY WHITE REPEATERS FROM THE RIVER WARDS, AND THE LIVING ARE TURNED AWAY. F1: the floater cars leaving the Burnham Hotel lot before dawn on election day (bn-scenario-003). F2: a repeater's slip with a ghost's name and address on it in Strode's hand (bn-scenario-003). F3: the Precinct 14 poll book: Lavinia Ransom's 'signature' in a hand that also signed for six other dead women (bn-scenario-003). F4: Mrs. Pauline Whitaker's list of living voters told 'You've already voted' (bn-scenario-003). F5: Amos Fairley's floater route (bn-scenario-002 or 003).

G. HORACE QUARTERMAN GAVE JULES UP, TO SAVE ZORA, AND THINKS HE CAN STILL MANAGE IT. G1: Zora Lattimore, if the party wins her trust: 'Uncle Horace told me to say nothing and he'd fix it' (bn-scenario-001 or 002). G2: the Vine Street Democratic Club's telephone log: a call to Police Headquarters at 4:02 a.m. Sunday (bn-scenario-002). G3: the numbers rumour about Jules came out of Quarterman's club (bn-scenario-001 or 002). G4: Quarterman himself, confronted with Jules's injuries (bn-scenario-002 or 003).

H. VARNUM HAS SENT FOR A PROFESSIONAL, AND THE MONEY LEADS TO HIS NEPHEW. H1: the back pages of the book: $11,400 in seven payments, initialled N.V. (whoever has the book). H2: Varnum Bonding's Wednesday wire to a St. Louis number, carried by Western Union's night messenger, a Lincoln High boy named Rudy Spurlock (bn-scenario-004). H3: the Muehlebach register: 'Everett Brumley, seed salesman, St. Louis', room paid by Varnum Bonding (bn-scenario-004). H4: Strode himself, frightened enough, names Norbert Varnum and the payments (bn-scenario-004). H5: Norbert Varnum's own bank deposit slips, carbon copies in the bonding company's files (bn-scenario-004).
controlFile.theBookAsKey: The players solve the case when they understand that Jules took the book and that the book is the ghost vote. Once they know that, every motive lines up: Strode needs it by Tuesday, Voyles needs it to make Jules disposable, Quarterman wants it burned to protect his people, Varnum wants it gone, and Merriwether wants it in court. Point clues A and B hard in bn-scenario-001. If the party reaches Wednesday without knowing about the book, have Zora Lattimore come to Matthias's office at night, or have Casey Dudek's employer say it out loud.
controlFile.outcomes: There is no single right ending, only consequences. JULES: rescued, he becomes a companion and the band plays again on Saturday night with its leader, bruised, at the piano; not rescued by Saturday 3 a.m., he dies on the river bluff, and the campaign carries that weight. THE BOOK: if the machine recovers it, Tuesday goes as planned. If the party holds it, Strode cannot run the ghost vote in the Second and Fourth Wards; he improvises from memory on Tuesday, badly, and the party can catch the repeaters in the act. ELECTION DAY: the machine wins regardless; it is 1936, and the margin is real enough without the ghosts. What changes is the evidence. THE RECKONING: the book can go to Agent Merriwether (who will prosecute; without Strode's testimony and the back pages explained, the case lands on the small men closest to hand, many of them Black precinct workers and floater drivers, and on the dead), to the Monitor (whose editor will print GHOST VOTE IN NEGRO WARDS unless Beatrice Albright or someone else forces the true story, that the ghosts are Black and the hands that voted them were white and paid from Main Street), to Horace Quarterman (who will burn it), or to Varnum (who will pay $5,000 and the Gold Leaf's licence for life). The best ending, and the hardest, gets Strode alive to Merriwether with the book, the back pages and Mrs. Whitaker's list, so that the case reaches Norbert Varnum and Lt. Voyles, and the names of the dead of Eighteenth Street are struck from the rolls. History did catch up with the city's machine politics in the following years, slowly, through federal courts; the campaign need not say how, only whether this book was part of it. Whatever happens, Lavinia Ransom's name should come off the register.
